notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Proverbs 19 (BSB), drawn from the sources I could access:

---

**v. 1: "Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a fool whose lips are perverse."**

The poor man of upright heart is contrasted with the rich fool who speaks twisted, deceitful things. The Hebrew word for "poor" (*rash*) is used in opposition to "rich," and Proverbs 28:6 confirms the contrast by adding "though he be rich." Gill notes the Syriac and Vulgate supply "rich man" explicitly. The poor man who lives a guileless, innocent life, content with his lot, is happier and better than the wealthy man whose words and actions are deceitful — his riches do not give him wisdom. Guzik notes that earlier proverbs criticized poverty caused by moral failure, but here Solomon recognizes that not all poverty stems from that. Waltke is quoted: "The poor may be miserable for the moment, but the unethical rich are miserable for eternity."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 2: "Even zeal is no good without knowledge, and he who hurries his footsteps misses the mark."**

The soul without knowledge — lacking practical wisdom and understanding of God — is in a bad state. The second line warns against rash haste: to act without deliberation is to sin or miss the mark. Delitzsch limits this to undisciplined pursuit of knowledge, but the Pulpit Commentary and others take it more generally: the ignorant person who acts hastily is sure to make grave mistakes. Gill adds that the Targum interprets this as being "swift with his feet to evil." The proverb echoes *festina lente* — "make haste slowly."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/

---

**v. 3: "A man's own folly subverts his way, yet his heart rages against the LORD."**

A person's own foolishness and self-will overturn and pervert his path in life. Yet instead of blaming himself, his heart frets and rages against God — charging God with the ruin that his own folly caused. Bridges calls this "the pride and blasphemy of a proud spirit. The criminal blames the judge for his righteous sentence." Ross notes that the fool "is not willing to accept failure as his own. To blame God is also folly." The Septuagint reads "he accuseth God in his heart."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 4: "Wealth attracts many friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend."**

Wealth multiplies friends, but these friendships are often insincere, drawn by what can be gained. The poor man is separated from his neighbor — his friend abandons him. The Pulpit Commentary notes this exposes human selfishness which the Mosaic Law sought to counteract (Deut. 15:7), and which Christianity fully addresses through the law of love. Waltke comments that each friend "forms the friendship out of what he can gain, not for what he can give."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 5: "A false witness will not go unpunished, and one who utters lies will not escape."**

The law court is primarily in view. The Law of Moses strictly forbade false witness (Ex. 20:16) and prescribed severe *lex talionis* penalties (Deut. 19:16–21). Yet even if human justice fails, God sees all and will not let the liar go unpunished. Gill adds that if not punished in this world, the false witness will be punished in the world to come. Kidner notes that this is "a statement made in faith, for perjurers may escape human justice" — citing Naboth and Jesus as examples.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 6: "Many seek the favor of the prince, and everyone is a friend of the gift giver."**

People flatter and entreat the favor of the powerful and liberal. The phrase "entreat the favor" literally means "stroke the face." Everyone wants to be the friend of someone who gives gifts. The Pulpit Commentary notes the LXX variant: "Every bad man is a reproach to a man" — meaning bad courtiers bring shame rather than glory to a prince.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 7: "All the brothers of a poor man hate him — how much more do his friends avoid him! He may pursue them with pleading, but they are nowhere to be found."**

This is one of the few tristichs (three-line verses) in the book. Even the poor man's own brothers despise him; how much more will his friends keep their distance. He pursues them with earnest entreaties, but his words and their promises alike come to nothing. Guzik contrasts this with Jesus, who "became poor (2 Cor. 8:9) to draw near to us in our poverty." The Hebrew text may be damaged; the LXX has an additional line, and scholars suggest a distich may have been lost.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 8: "He who acquires wisdom loves himself; one who safeguards understanding will find success."**

The Hebrew word for "wisdom" here is *leb*, literally "heart" — wisdom is a matter not of intellect alone but of the will and affections. To pursue wisdom is to love one's own soul; the opposite is to hate oneself (Prov. 29:24). Gill adds a spiritual application: the one who gets "a new heart" — a heart of flesh, tender and contrite — shows true regard for his immortal soul. Keeping understanding (guarding it like treasure) leads to finding good both now and hereafter.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 9: "A false witness will not go unpunished, and one who pours out lies will perish."**

A near-repetition of v. 5, but sharper: the liar will not merely "not escape" but will "perish." Guzik ties this to Revelation 21:8, where liars have their part in the lake of fire. Gill notes it applies to those who speak doctrinal lies and are given up to believe them (2 Thess. 2:11).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 10: "Luxury is unseemly for a fool — how much worse for a slave to rule over princes!"**

Luxury and delicate living are ruinous for a fool, who lacks the wisdom to use prosperity properly. Far worse is the situation of a slave or servant elevated to rule over princes — an observation also made in Prov. 30:22 and Eccl. 10:6–7. The Pulpit Commentary notes the "beggar on horseback" theme: a low-born person suddenly raised to power often becomes an unbearable despot. Guzik remarks that "this is one of the proverbs that the gospel and the new covenant turns on its head, where those who would be great should be as servants and not as princes (Matt. 20:26)."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 11: "A man's insight gives him patience, and his virtue is to overlook an offense."**

A wise and discreet person is slow to anger, taking time to consider the offense rather than reacting immediately. It is a person's glory — true honor — to pass over a transgression rather than insist on settling every account. In this, the forgiving person imitates God (Micah 7:18). Trapp says, "The manlier any man is, the milder and readier to pass by an offence. This shows that he hath much of God in him." McKane describes it as "the ability to shrug off insults and the absence of a brooding hypersensitivity."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 12: "A king's rage is like the roar of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass."**

The anger of a king — especially an Eastern despot — is as terrifying as a young lion's roar, signaling approaching destruction. By contrast, his favor is life-giving and refreshing, like the dew essential to vegetation in Palestine's dry summer. Gaebelein applies this spiritually to Christ, the Lion of Judah: "Some day He will roar in His displeasure … but even then His grace will be revealed, for in wrath He will remember mercy." Guzik adds that while the king's favor is refreshing like dew, it can also be fleeting like dew — whereas God's favor is not fleeting.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 13: "A foolish son is his father's ruin, and a quarrelsome wife is like a constant dripping."**

A foolish son brings multiple sorrows (*calamities* is plural in Hebrew) upon his father. The contentious wife is compared to the incessant dripping of rain through a leaky flat roof — an ever-present annoyance that erodes and destroys. Kidner relays an Arab proverb: "Three things make a house intolerable: *tak* (the leaking through of rain), *nak* (a wife's nagging) and *bak* (bugs)." Clarke remarks: "God help the man who is in such a case, with house or wife!"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 14: "Houses and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD."**

Houses and riches can come to any man — worthy or not — through earthly inheritance. But a prudent, wise wife is a special gift from God and surpasses all material inheritance. The LXX renders it, "It is by the Lord that a man is matched with a woman," emphasizing divine providence in marriage. Trapp says, "Nature makes a woman, election a wife; but to be prudent, wise, and virtuous is of the Lord." Ross adds: "When a marriage turns out well, one should credit God."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 15: "Laziness brings on deep sleep, and an idle soul will suffer hunger."**

The Hebrew word for "deep sleep" (*tardemah*) is the same used for the supernatural sleep God cast upon Adam (Gen. 2:21) — implying profound insensibility. Laziness creates a vicious cycle: it enervates a person, rendering them as useless as if asleep, and leads to more laziness. The idle person will inevitably suffer hunger. Waltke notes that the sluggard's "fate is similar to that of drunkards and gluttons (Prov. 23:21)."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 16: "He who keeps a commandment preserves his soul, but he who is careless in his ways will die."**

Obedience to God's commandments guards a person's natural and spiritual life. The one who is careless — who despises his own ways and pays no heed to whether they please God — will die. Ellicott adds that this death can be physical, spiritual, and ultimately the second death (Rev. 2:11). Guzik frames it simply: "God gave His commandment to give us life and to keep us from death."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 17: "Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender."**

This is one of the most striking promises in Proverbs. To show pity on the poor is to make God Himself the debtor. Clarke exclaims: "O what a word is this! God makes himself debtor for every thing that is given to the poor! Who would not advance much upon such credit?" Meyer adds, "God will never be in your debt. He is exact and punctilious in His repayment." Ross clarifies that "this promise of reward does not necessarily signify that he will get his money back; the rewards in Proverbs involve life and prosperity in general." Guzik notes that the promise echoes Jesus' words in Matthew 25:40 — what is done for the least is done for Christ.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 18: "Discipline your son, for in that there is hope; do not be party to his death."**

Parents must discipline their children while there is still hope — the window of opportunity is limited. The second line is debated: some render it "do not set your heart on his destruction" (i.e., do not go so far as to kill him in excessive zeal, per Eph. 6:4); others read "let not thy soul spare for his crying" — do not let his tears deter you from proper chastisement. Bridges says: "It is far better that the child should cry under healthy correction than that parents should later cry under the bitter fruit … of neglected discipline." Waltke adds that if parents fail to use "the God-given means of verbal reproof … and corporal punishment," they are "unwittingly party to the worst punishment, his death."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 19: "A man of great anger must pay the penalty; if you rescue him, you will have to do so again."**

A person of uncontrolled, fiery temper repeatedly lands himself in trouble and suffers punishment — much of it self-inflicted. If you rescue him from one mess, you will have to do it again and again, because the root problem is his character, not his circumstances. Kidner puts it succinctly: "An ungovernable temper will repeatedly land its owner in fresh trouble." Constable notes that "the hothead must be corrected by allowing the consequences of his own foibles to punish him."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 20: "Listen to counsel and accept discipline, that you may be wise the rest of your days."**

A teachable spirit — willingness to hear counsel and receive correction — is the first mark of wisdom. Gill applies this to the counsel of Christ, the Wonderful Counsellor, and the Scriptures "which are able to make a man wise unto salvation." The goal is to be wise "in thy latter end" — at life's close, showing that one has lived wisely regarding eternal things. Gaebelein poignantly notes that Solomon himself failed to heed this, becoming a fool in his latter days (1 Kings 11:11).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 21: "Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail."**

Human beings naturally devise many plans and schemes. Yet over against all these stands the unchangeable counsel of the LORD, which alone will stand. Guzik quotes James 4:13–15: "Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that.'" Morgan calls this "a perfectly self-evident assertion, but, as such, important as to warrant a pause in reading it." The Geneva Bible note adds: "Man's device will not have success, unless God governs it, whose purpose is unchangeable."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 22: "The desire of a man is loving devotion; better to be poor than a liar."**

The Hebrew is difficult. Ellicott explains: what makes a man desired or beloved is his kindness (*chesed*, loving devotion). A poor man who would do a kindness if only he could is better than a rich liar who could help but professes inability. The Geneva Bible glosses it: "The poor man who is honest is to be esteemed above the rich who is not virtuous." Guzik warns that kindness, though valuable, must not be treated as the only virtue — truth matters, too.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 23: "The fear of the LORD leads to life, that one may rest content, without visitation from harm."**

The fear of the LORD — reverent awe and submission — leads to true life and lasting satisfaction. The promise "he shall not be visited with evil" reflects the OT covenant promise of protection (Lev. 26:6). Ellicott notes that the New Testament offers a higher blessing: not immunity from all trouble, but protection in it (Rom. 8:28, 35–39). Gaebelein observes that Solomon enjoyed this as long as the fear of the LORD governed him, but when he turned away, evil came upon his kingdom.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 24: "The slacker buries his hand in the dish; he will not even bring it back to his mouth."**

A humorous but pointed hyperbole. The "dish" is the common bowl at an Oriental meal into which diners dipped their hands. The lazy man is so sluggish that, having put his hand in the dish, he cannot muster the energy to lift the food to his mouth. Constable notes the point: "a lazy person will bear the consequences of his own laziness."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 25: "Strike a mocker, and the simple will beware; rebuke the discerning man, and he will gain knowledge."**

The "mocker" (scorner) is beyond correction — reproof is wasted on him (Prov. 9:7; 13:1). Yet punishing him serves as a warning to the "simple" (the impressionable, not yet hardened). By contrast, the discerning person profits from mere verbal rebuke — he "will understand knowledge." Ellicott notes that God at first punishes sinners for their own good, then, when they become obdurate, as a warning to others (Amos 4:6–12).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 26: "He who assaults his father or evicts his mother is a son who brings shame and disgrace."**

The son who violently mistreats his parents — assaulting his father or driving out his mother — is a shameful, disgraceful wretch. This is a worst-case picture of the "foolish son" described in v. 13. The verse intensifies the call to honor parents from the fifth commandment.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 27: "If you cease to hear instruction, my son, you will stray from the words of knowledge."**

Here begins a section using "my son" address, echoing the opening chapters. The warning is stark: stop listening to sound instruction and you will inevitably drift away from the words of knowledge. Ellicott offers an alternative rendering: "Cease to hear instruction if you are only going to err afterwards — better not know the truth than learn it only to desert it" (cf. 2 Peter 2:21).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/proverbs-19.html

---

**v. 28: "A corrupt witness mocks justice, and a wicked mouth swallows iniquity."**

The "worthless" (ungodly) witness scorns the very concept of justice, despising the law's commands against perjury (Ex. 20:16). The wicked person devours iniquity like a tasty morsel (cf. Prov. 18:8 — the same imagery of swallowing evil as a delicacy).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

---

**v. 29: "Judgments are prepared for mockers, and beatings for the backs of fools."**

The chapter closes with certainty of judgment. Scorners and fools will not escape: judgments (divine and human) are prepared, fixed, and ready for them. Gill connects this to the "everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matt. 25:41). The Geneva Bible and JFB concur: their punishment is sure and appointed.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/19.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/proverbs/19.htm

---

## Notes on Differing Traditions and Other Views

Within the sources I could access, explicit denominational disputes on Proverbs 19 were limited. However, the following are worth noting:

**On v. 10 ("a slave to rule over princes"):** Guzik (broadly evangelical/Pentecostal-charismatic) explicitly notes that "this is one of the proverbs that the gospel and the new covenant turns on its head," referencing Matthew 20:26 where greatness is found in servanthood. Older commentators (Pulpit, Ellicott, Gill) treat this as straightforward social wisdom without that theological inversion.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/

**On v. 17 ("lends to the LORD"):** All traditions agree on the core meaning — generosity to the poor brings God's blessing. Ross (cited by Guzik) notes that "this promise of reward does not necessarily signify that he will get his money back," which implicitly counters any prosperity-gospel reading that would treat this as a guaranteed financial return.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/

**On v. 18 ("discipline your son"):** Waltke (evangelical/Reformed) explicitly endorses "corporal punishment" as a God-given means. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) agrees that "yasser includes chastisement as well as instruction." Ellicott balances with the warning from Eph. 6:4 and Col. 3:21 not to provoke children to wrath. No source from the approved list directly argues against corporal discipline, though some modern Christian traditions do.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-19.html

**On v. 21 ("the LORD's counsel will stand"):** The Geneva Bible notes emphasize divine sovereignty: "Man's device will not have success, unless God governs it, whose purpose is unchangeable" — reflecting a Reformed view of providence. Guzik balances this with James 4:13–15, emphasizing that man should plan but in humble submission to God's will. The Expositor's Bible Commentary frames this as the futility of human schemes apart from God.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/proverbs-19.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-19/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/proverbs-19.html

**On v. 23 ("without visitation from harm"):** The OT promise of physical protection is noted by Ellicott as an Israelite covenant blessing, but he adds that the NT offers "a higher blessing … not immunity from trouble … but protection in it" (Rom. 8:28, 35). This distinction between old-covenant physical protection and new-covenant spiritual protection through trials is a point where some Word of Faith teaching would differ, claiming the physical promise directly for believers today — though no source in my search results explicitly addresses this debate for this verse.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/19.htm

**On Catholic / Orthodox readings:** I was unable to fetch pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org due to tool limits. The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott (Anglican) occasionally reference the Vulgate and Septuagint readings, which are respected in Catholic and Orthodox traditions, but I cannot report distinct Catholic or Orthodox interpretations from those sites directly.
